name: Mulberry extract
lead: Mulberry extract is a plant extract from trees of the genus Morus, marketed in skincare as a botanical brightener, with mulberroside F named as its skin-lightening constituent. The fruit and leaves are also sold as dietary supplements [1].

The material reviewed here contains no human study of topical mulberry extract for skin tone. Published mulberry research concerns other uses: blood-glucose effects, antioxidant chemistry and food science.
infobox: Topical brightening ingredient; also food colorant and supplement [1]

paras: Mulberry trees are grown for fruit, for leaves that feed silkworms (especially white mulberry), for bark used in papermaking and for folk medicine [1]. Anthocyanins can be extracted from the fruit and used as natural food colorants [1]. Fruit and leaf products are sold as supplements [1]. The Wikipedia article on mulberry does not mention skin lightening or mulberroside F [1].

In cosmetics, mulberry extract is positioned as a plant-derived alternative to synthetic brighteners, with mulberroside F cited by marketers and enthusiasts as the active compound. No published trial in the sources reviewed tests it on human skin.
No studies found on topical mulberry extract for skin brightening or hyperpigmentation.

Related work concerns different uses. A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study reported that an oral mulberry extract improved glucose tolerance and lowered insulin concentrations in adults with normal blood sugar [2]. Several registered trials examine mulberry leaf extract for blood glucose [3][4]. Laboratory studies have compared the antioxidant capacity of black and white mulberry extracts in cell models [5]. None addresses skin pigmentation.

card.summary: A botanical 'brightener' whose published research is about blood sugar and antioxidants, not skin tone.
card.note: No human skin-brightening trial was found in the sources reviewed.

quick.overview:
Mulberry extract comes from Morus trees and is sold in skincare as a plant brightener, with mulberroside F named as the active compound.

The studies found concern other uses, mainly blood glucose and antioxidant chemistry. No human trial of it for skin tone turned up.
quick.mechanism: Cosmetic marketing attributes brightening to mulberroside F. The sources reviewed do not document a mechanism in human skin.
quick.risks: No skin-specific safety data were found. Mulberry fruit and leaf are common food and supplement ingredients.
